entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adad-guppi, a devoted follower of the moon god Sîn in the northern Assyrian city of Harran, played a pivotal role in the religious landscape of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

Born into a family of priestesses, Adad-guppi was appointed as the chief priestess of Sîn at the Harranian temple, where she oversaw the daily rituals and ceremonies.

As the mother of King Nabonidus, who ruled from 555 to 539 BCE and attempted to revive the ancient Assyrian traditions of his ancestors, Adad-guppi held significant influence over the king's decisions.

The Harranian priestesses of Sîn, including Adad-guppi, held substantial spiritual authority, which helped maintain the stability of the empire.

Adad-guppi's legacy extends beyond her own time, as her devotion to Sîn and her role in shaping the Neo-Babylonian Empire have left a lasting impact on the religious and cultural landscape of the ancient Near East.

In the words of the ancient Assyrian priestly text, 'She who was appointed as the chief priestess of Sîn, she who held the sacred power, she who was the mother of the king, she who was the one who maintained the balance of the universe.'
